findings.title: A callee another package can supply is counted by nobody at the library's own line (extends O1 to summaries and contract verdicts)
findings.program:
# package `bus`, a library compiled once
pub type Handler = fn()
static mut HANDLERS: Array[Handler] = []

pub fn add(owns h: Handler):
    HANDLERS.push(owns h)

@noalloc
pub fn run_all():
    for h in HANDLERS:          # walks HANDLERS
        h()                     # <- BREAKS: [EFF-2] counts the functions `bus` stores into Handler places (none reshape HANDLERS, none allocate): no E3020, no E4001, and the line is compiled once

# package `app`
from bus import add, run_all
fn main():
    add(owns fn(): add(owns fn(): pass))   # a handler that adds a handler (and allocates)
    run_all()                               # h() runs `add`: HANDLERS grows and moves its buffer under the walk; the loop reads freed memory. The same with a `virtual` method of a `pub` class, or a `dyn I` of a `pub` interface, whose override `app` writes.
findings.why: [EFF-2]: "For a field, a list element, a parameter or a local of a function type, it is every lambda and named function the program puts in that place, a library's included (verdict 122)" and "For an interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method, it is every implementation and override the program has": a whole-program fact, unknown when `bus` is compiled. [EFF-4]: "the function values the package stores into a function type and the callbacks it hands to C, which a program that uses the package counts wherever such a value is called": the dependant counts the library's stores at the dependant's lines; nothing says what the library's own `h()` line counts for the stores a dependant will make, and [EFF-25] decides `E3020` at that line "and nothing is checked while the program runs". [BRW-18] says the walk is `E3020` "through any call that may change it", judged by the summary the library computed. [EFF-6] checks a contract "over the whole reachable call graph", which the library cannot see. O1 covers layout and code ([OBJ-1], [THR-2], [WK-18]); this is the same shape for the summaries and the contract verdicts.
findings.proposed_text:
Add after `[EFF-2]`:

* `[EFF-2a]` **A callee another package can supply.** Inside the package that declares them, a place of a function type that another package can store into (a parameter of a `pub` function, a `pub` field, a `pub` `static`, an element of a list or map such a place holds, and every place a value from one of them is copied into), a `virtual` method of a `pub` class and a method of a `pub` interface called through `dyn` have, beside the functions this package stores or declares there (`[EFF-2]`), the functions another package may put there: such a call counts as calling every `pub` function of this package, as changing every place a `pub` name of this package reaches (a `pub static mut`; the fields of an object a `pub` function is given, returns or holds), and as having every effect the place's type's contracts do not exclude. A place or method no other package can reach keeps `[EFF-2]`'s rule. The message names the route: `E3020` "`h()` (line 11) may add to `HANDLERS` (through `add`, which a function another package stores into a `Handler` may call) while this loop walks `HANDLERS` (line 10); run from a list of your own: write `todo = mem.take(ref mut HANDLERS)` above line 10, `for h in todo:` in place of line 10, and `HANDLERS.extend(owns todo)` below the loop"; `E4001` "`run_all` is `@noalloc`, and `h()` (line 11) may run a function another package stores into a `Handler`, which may allocate; say what a `Handler` may do: write `@noalloc` above `type Handler = fn()`". A dependant's own stores are counted by the dependant at its own lines (`[EFF-4]`), and `[DET-3]` counts them the same way.
findings.touches_owner_verdict: 122 (kept inside a package; the edge rule adds the unseen stores, it does not return to the by-type rule)
findings.milestone: M6a (summaries at the package edge; the contract half in M11)
findings.codes: E3020, E4001 (and each contract's code) reused; shape: the chain names the `pub` route another package may use

findings.title: A `weakref` link to an object made `using` an arena survives the arena's reset or end, and opens a reused block
findings.program:
class Node:
    value: int
class Other:
    name: String

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(4096)
    w: weakref Node = None
    if true:
        n = Node(value=1) using frame   # the object's block lies in `frame`, whose `deallocate` does nothing ([ALC-1] (1))
        w = weakref n                   # weak count 1
    # `n` ended here: its drop ran; [WK-11] keeps the block for `w`, but giving it back is a no-op
    frame.reset()                       # <- BREAKS: allowed, no value made in `frame` lives ([ALC-5]); the bytes are reusable
    o = Other(name=String("x")) using frame   # placed where `n`'s block was
    if w exists as p:                   # [WK-12]: one test of the header at that address, which is `o`'s, live
        println(p.value)                # `p: Node` reads an `Other`
findings.why: [ALC-5]: "While a value made in a memory manager's instance lives, the instance is changed only by ...": `n` has ended. [LT-4]: "A value made in a memory manager's instance ..., and every value that holds one, lives no longer than that instance": a `weakref` link holds no value (IX.0: ownership "none"; [HEAP-7]). [WK-11]: "the block is freed when the weak count reaches 0", but in a manager whose `deallocate` does nothing the block is "freed together when the instance is cleared or ends" ([ALC-1] (1)) whatever the weak count. [ARN-1]: `reset()` "ends every view into the arena", and a link is not a view. The same with the arena's end while `w` lives, and with a `FoundByAddress` pool that is cleared.
findings.proposed_text:
Add after `[ALC-5]`:

* `[ALC-5a]` **A link holds the block.** A `weakref` link to a value made in a memory manager's instance counts, for `[LT-4]` and `[ALC-5]`, as a value that holds one, since the target's block stays until the link ends (`[WK-11]`): the link carries the instance's region from the line that makes it (`w = weakref n`) through every place it is copied or stored, as a kept view does (`[LT-45]`); keeping it where it would outlive the instance is `E3063` ("`w` links to a `Node` made in `frame` (line 10), and `frame` ends when `main` returns; end the link first: write `w = None` above the return"), and while it lives a change of the instance that `[ALC-5]` does not allow is `E3021` ("`frame.reset()` (line 13) reuses the memory of the `Node` that `w` links to (made in `frame` on line 10), and `w` is used on line 15; end the link first: write `w = None` above line 13"). Nothing runs for this: the block a link keeps is given back by the manager's own `deallocate` when the weak count reaches 0, as any other.

findings.title: A `thread_shared` value made `using` an arena is queued past the end of its compile-time life, and the arena is reset before the check point that ends it
findings.program:
struct Big:
    data: Array[u8]

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(1 << 20)
    v = thread_shared Big(data=[0, 1, 2]) using frame   # made by the main thread: its block (header and `Big`) lies in `frame`; `data`'s buffer is `Global`'s
    with scope:
        scope.spawn(fn() [owns v]:        # the owner the main thread counted at home goes to the task ([THR-17])
            mem.drop(owns v))             # ends on the task's thread: the away count goes below zero, `v` is queued for the main thread ([RC-4] point 2)
    # the scope's end joins the task; the main thread's check point was BEFORE the blocking call ([RC-4] point 3): the queue now holds `v`, "intact"
    frame.reset()                         # <- BREAKS: allowed, no value made in `frame` lives at this line ([ALC-5] is checked when compiling); `v`'s bytes are reusable
    buf = ref mut frame.alloc_zeroed[u8](4096)   # overwrites `v`'s header and its `data` pointer
    for i in 0..10:                       # the loop's back edge is the next check point: `v` is ended here, its `data` pointer read from reused bytes and freed
        buf[i] = 1
findings.why: [RC-4] point 3: check points are placed "at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends": none after the join. Point 5: "it is ended at its making thread's next check point. Until then it is intact". [ALC-5]: "While a value made in a memory manager's instance lives ... any other change ... is `E3021`", decided when compiling, where `v`'s life ends at the join. [LT-4] bounds the value's life by the instance, and the runtime keeps it alive longer than the compiler's bound. The value cannot reach an unscoped thread (its instance word is a `sharedref mut` link, [LT-4], [THR-8]), so the scoped task's join is the one path.
findings.proposed_text:
In `[RC-4]` point 3, replace "The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends." with:

"The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before and after every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, a `join`, the end of a `with scope` block, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends. The one after a `join` or a scope's end is what makes a value a task ended on its own thread end before the parent's next line: nothing a joined task queued is still waiting when the parent runs on."

And add to `[ALC-5]`: "A `thread_shared` value lives, for this rule, until the check point that ends it (`[RC-4]` point 5): with the check point after every join, that is before the parent's next line, so the rule is checked as written."
findings.milestone: M9 (the check points), with M10's arena check
findings.codes: none new; the runtime's check-point placement; a `[COST-3]` row note: one queue test after each join

findings.title: "Which thread made a value" is read from a memory-chunk header that `malloc`, a replaced global allocator, a host allocator and a `using` manager do not have (extends O8)
findings.program:
# any program whose `thread_shared` blocks do not come from a runtime chunk: today every program ([RT-1] allocates with `malloc`), one with `[build] global_allocator = "alloc.POOL"` ([ALC-3]), an embedded one ([FFI-27]), and this one:
unsafe extend Pool implements Allocator:   # the program's own manager; a `# SAFETY:` note above
    ...

fn main():
    pool = Pool.with_capacity(1 << 20)
    v = thread_shared Big(data=[0]) using pool    # the block comes from `pool.allocate(...)`: memory no runtime chunk holds
    with scope:
        scope.spawn(fn():
            mine = thread_shared v)               # <- BREAKS: the +1 asks which thread made `v` and reads "the header of the chunk its block came from"; there is none, so the bytes before the block (another value, or `Pool`'s bookkeeping) answer. A wrong answer counts this task's owner in the home count with plain instructions, racing the main thread's: a lost update frees `v` while owned.
findings.why: [OBJ-1]: "Which thread made a value is read from the header of the memory chunk its block came from, written once when the chunk is made, never from the value." [RT-1]: "Allocation uses the system `malloc`/`realloc`/`free`": the runtime lays out no chunk (`runtime/ember_rt/src/ember_rt.c`'s only `chunk` is a parallel loop's). [ALC-1]: a `thread_shared` value may be made `using` any `Allocator`, whose memory the runtime never sees; [ALC-3] and [FFI-27] replace `Global` itself. O8 asks what happens when a chunk is reused; this is the case where the chunk does not exist.
findings.proposed_text:
In `[OBJ-1]`, replace "Which thread made a value is read from the header of the memory chunk its block came from, written once when the chunk is made, never from the value." with:

"Which thread made a `thread_shared` value is written into the value's own header at the line that makes it, one store, and read from there by every thread that adds or subtracts an owner, one load: the 32-byte header holds its five numbers in 20 bytes, and the making thread's identity takes 8 of the 12 left (`[RC-4]`). It is never read from the memory around the block, which may be `malloc`'s (`[RT-1]`), a host's (`[FFI-27]`), a replaced global allocator's (`[ALC-3]`) or a `using` manager's (`[ALC-1]`), none of which the runtime lays out."

In the `[RC-4]` header table add the row `20  8  maker  tid  the thread that made it, written once at the making line`, and in `[COST-3]`'s `thread_shared` row: "one store of the making thread at the making line, read on the away path".
findings.touches_owner_verdict: 101 (the header's content, not its size: 32 bytes stays)

findings.title: "needs drop" is used by six rules and defined nowhere
findings.why: [ARN-2]: "an `alloc*` of a type that needs drop is `E3090`"; [ARN-3]: "requires `T` not to need drop"; [ARN-5]: "Their elements, keys and values must not need drop"; [ARN-8]: "for a `T` that needs drop" the operations are unsafe, "for a `T` with nothing to drop they stay safe". The glossary (Appendix F) has no row for it, and [DRP-8] speaks of "a value whose type has a `drop`", which reads as the method. [PHIL-10] promises that a program "cannot end a value without its clean-up": here the value is never ended at all, its clean-up never runs, and the same words let a count leak.
findings.proposed_text: Add to the glossary (Appendix F): "| **needs drop** | a type whose values do something when they end: one with a `fn drop()`, a heap type (`String`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `owns T`), a class object, a counted owner or link (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`), a guard, a function value with state, an `owns dyn I`, a foreign type with a destructor, and every struct, enum, tuple or fixed array with a field or element that does; a type that is `Copy`, a `ref`, a span, a `StrView`, a raw pointer and a `sharedref mut` link never do. A `MaybeUninit[T]` never does, whatever `T` is (`[ARN-8]`) |". In `[ARN-2]` write "a type that needs drop (Appendix F)" at the first use, and in `[ARN-3]` after `alloc_uninit[T](n)`: "for a `T` that needs drop too, since what `write_at` puts there is dropped by nobody, `E3090` as well, whose help names `owns T using frame`".
findings.milestone: M10 (the arena check reads the fact; the fact itself is M3's drop glue)

findings.title: Whether a value made `using` an instance carries `Alloc`, and which panic its failure is, is unsaid
findings.why: X.1's table: `Alloc` is introduced by "a value put in its own block by `owns`, `shares` or `thread_shared`" and "arena growth", with no word on the instance; [HEAP-1]: "carries the `Alloc` effect where it allocates"; [ARN-4]: `FixedArena` "carries no `Alloc` on allocation, and panics on exhaustion (`try_alloc` returns `Option`)" and "is the arena for `@noalloc` code"; the table's `Panic(Explicit)` row lists "allocation failure"; [EFF-16]: "forbids only the panics the programmer writes and allocation failure" and names "exhaustion outside `Alloc`" as what the model does not cover; [ALC-2] says `allocate` is "null on failure" and nothing of what the compiler's own call does then; [ALC-4] speaks of standard containers only.
findings.proposed_text:
Add to `[ALC-1]` (or as `[ALC-6]`):

* `[ALC-6]` **A making line has its instance's effects.** A line that makes a value `using x`, and every growth and end of that value, carries the effects of the `Allocator` methods it calls on `x`'s type (`[EFF-1]`), and `Alloc` is the effect of `Global`'s and `System`'s `allocate` and `reallocate`, of `ember_alloc`, and of every implementation that reaches them: a value made in a `FixedArena` carries no `Alloc`; one made in an `Arena` carries it (growth, `[ARN-4]`). When the instance's `allocate` or `reallocate` returns null, the compiler's own call panics, "out of memory", the panic `Panic(Explicit)` lists as allocation failure, as a `FixedArena`'s exhaustion is (`[ARN-4]`): under `@nopanic(explicit)` the forms are `try_alloc`, `try_reserve` and `try_push` (`[ALC-4]`), and a making line `using x` there is `E4040` whose help names `x.try_alloc`. `reallocate` that returns null leaves the old block as it was.

findings.title: No rule says how a compiler knows that an `alloc*` result is a place of its own, or what a user-written arena's `alloc` is
findings.program:
fn build(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    a = ref mut frame.alloc_zeroed[int](8)   # a `ref mut` view whose result "points into" `frame` ([LT-1]: an arena is a source parameter)
    b = ref mut frame.alloc_zeroed[int](8)   # <- by [BRW-1] a second change of `frame` while `a`, a `ref mut` view into it, is used: `E3021`, as `xs.get_mut(1)` while `xs.get_mut(0)` lives is. [ARN-1] says the opposite, by fiat for `Arena`. And for the program's own arena:
    a[0] = 1
    b[0] = 2
    return a[0] + b[0]

struct MyArena:
    buf: MutSpan[u8]
    top: int
    fn alloc(ref mut this, n: int) -> MutSpan[u8]:   # the same shape in the program's own code
        s = ref mut this.buf[this.top .. this.top + n]
        this.top += n
        return s                                     # points into `this.buf`: a part of `this`, so two of these are two `ref mut` names of one field: the compiler must treat it as the std's `Arena` or as an ordinary method, and the text says which for neither
findings.why: [ARN-1]: "Each gives a view of memory that no earlier view of the arena reaches, and the views point into the arena's memory, not into its cursor: an `alloc*` call ends no earlier view and overlaps none, so many allocations are outstanding at once, each a place of its own" and `reset()` "ends every view": facts about `Arena` with no mechanism by which a compiler derives them from the type's code or distinguishes `alloc` from `reset` (both write fields of `this`). [LT-1] makes the result point into `this`; [BRW-1] makes a `ref mut` name the only name of its place while used; [EFF-24]'s summary lists no fact that says "a result that is a place of its own". A compiler built from the text alone must either special-case `std.arena` or refuse `build`.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[ARN-1]`: "These facts are the compiler's own for the types of `std.arena` (`Arena`, `FixedArena`, `ScopedArena`, `ThreadArena`), as `ref_to_ptr` is one function it knows (§IV.5): an `alloc*` result lives no longer than the arena (`[LT-1]`) and is a place of its own for `[BRW-1]`, reached through no field of the arena and overlapping no other result; `reset()`, `scope()`'s end for the scope's results, and the arena's end are the operations that end them. No other type gets them: a method of the program's own type that returns a view of its object is an ordinary method, whose result points into `this` and is exclusive with it (`[LT-1]`, `[BRW-1]`), and a manager of the program's own is used through `Allocator` and `using` (`[ALC-1]`), whose values are places of their own by `[ALC-5]`."
findings.codes: none new; E3021 stays the code for the ordinary method's second view

findings.title: `[DSJ-5]`'s "unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint" is a proof `[EFF-15]`'s closed list does not contain
findings.why: [DSJ-5]: "Both forms record a `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` site whose reason is `establishes_static_fact` (`[EFF-11]`), unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint, in which case no comparison is emitted." [EFF-15]: "The proofs that count are exactly those this document specifies — `[OPT-2]`, `[RNG-4]`, `[SIMD-7]` and the parent-link proof of Part VIII" and "a verdict is computed as if every one of them were applied wherever its conditions hold". [EFF-9] makes the site the effect. "already knows" names no rule.
findings.proposed_text:
In `[DSJ-5]`, replace "unless the compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint, in which case no comparison is emitted" with: "unless the two views are known apart by `[DSJ-11]`, in which case no site is recorded and no comparison is emitted". Add:

* `[DSJ-11]` **Views known apart.** Two views are known apart, with no compare, exactly when they are the two results of one `split_at`, `split_at_mut`, `get_pair_mut` or `chunks_mut` call (the same call, by its position), two columns of one SoA, two `alloc*` results of one arena (`[ARN-1]`), or views of two different whole variables neither of which is reached through the other; nothing else is, whatever the compiler could see. This is the one disjointness proof, and `[EFF-15]`'s list names it.

In `[EFF-15]` replace "`[OPT-2]`, `[RNG-4]`, `[SIMD-7]` and the parent-link proof of Part VIII" with "`[OPT-2]`, `[RNG-4]`, `[SIMD-7]`, `[DSJ-11]` and the parent-link proof of Part VIII".
findings.milestone: M6c (alias facts), the verdict in M11

findings.title: `std.mem.copy` and `copy_nonoverlapping` write through raw pointers and no rule says they are `unsafe fn`s
findings.program:
from std.mem import copy_nonoverlapping

fn main():
    src = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    dst = [0]
    p = ref_to_ptr(ref src[0])          # safe (§IV.5, ODR-075)
    q = ref_to_ptr(ref mut dst[0])      # safe
    copy_nonoverlapping(p, q, 4)        # <- a call of a function, not a read through `*T`, and not in [UNS-1]'s list: if `std.mem` declares it a plain `fn`, safe code writes three elements past `dst`
findings.why: [UNS-1] lists what needs an unsafe context: dereference, offset, casts, "call an `unsafe fn`", `transmute`, `get_unchecked`, `assume_init`, `assume_disjoint`, `into_raw()`, `MaybeUninit` of a drop type, unsafe implementations; `copy` and `copy_nonoverlapping` are not there, and [UNS-5] only lists them beside `Volatile`, whose reads [STD-29] does declare `unsafe fn`s. [UNS-7]: "The standard library carries `@safety` on every unsafe function it exports" says nothing about which these are. The text is the only authority for the std's declarations ([STD-*]), so a compiler and a std built from it may declare them safe.
findings.proposed_text: Replace `[UNS-5]`'s text with: "`std.mem` provides `Volatile[*T]` (volatile reads and writes, `[STD-29]`), `transmute[A, B]`, `copy` and `copy_nonoverlapping` (which read and write through the raw pointers they are given), `zeroed[T]()` (requires `T: needs Zeroable`) and `MaybeUninit`. `transmute`, `copy` and `copy_nonoverlapping` are `unsafe fn`s (`[UNS-1]`): a call of one outside unsafe code is `E3100` ("`copy_nonoverlapping(p, q, 4)` (line 8) writes through the raw pointer `q`, and nothing checks that four `int`s are writable there; put line 8 in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note saying why that holds here"), and each carries `@safety` (`[UNS-7]`). `zeroed`, `swap`, `replace`, `take`, `drop` and `keep_alive` are safe." In `[UNS-1]`'s list, after `transmute` write "`copy` or `copy_nonoverlapping`".
findings.milestone: text only (std.mem's declarations; `E3100`'s path exists), listed by `ember tcb` in M12

findings.title: `[DET-2]`'s closed list of `Nondet` sources misses every read whose value depends on which thread acted first
findings.program:
@deterministic
fn gather() -> Array[int]:
    (tx, rx) = channel[int]()
    out: Array[int] = []
    with scope:
        a = thread_shared tx
        scope.spawn(fn(): a.send(owns 1))
        scope.spawn(fn(): tx.send(owns 2))
        out.push(owns rx.recv())        # <- the first of two senders on two threads: 1 or 2 by the scheduler; not in [DET-2]'s list, so no E4070
        out.push(owns rx.recv())
    return out                          # [1, 2] on one run, [2, 1] on the next; the same with `m.try_lock()`'s answer, or an `Atomic` read of a counter a running task adds to
findings.why: [DET-2]: "`Nondet` is introduced by exactly: ...; the wall clock, the monotonic clock, the system random source, thread and job completion order; ...". A receive is a channel operation (`Sync + Block`), not "completion order"; `try_lock`'s answer and an `Atomic` read of another thread's writes are named nowhere. [DET-3] counts only what [DET-2] lists. The word "exactly" closes the list, so a compiler must accept `gather`.
findings.proposed_text: In `[DET-2]`, after "thread and job completion order;" insert: "a read whose value depends on which thread acted first: a receive on a channel that more than one thread may send to, `try_lock`'s and `try_recv`'s answer, a lock's view or an `Atomic` read of a place a thread or task that has not been joined may change (after the join, the place is what the joined tasks left, in spawn order for a reduction, `[THR-21]`);". `E4070`'s message for it: "`gather` is `@deterministic`, and `rx.recv()` (line 9) receives from a channel two threads send to (lines 7 and 8), so which value comes first differs between runs; give each task its own result and join them in order: write `h1 = scope.spawn(...)`, `h2 = scope.spawn(...)` returning the values, and `out.push(owns h1.join())`, `out.push(owns h2.join())`".

findings.title: A generator's `next` "carries the effects of the body up to the next `yield`": which segment runs is a run-time state
findings.program:
gen fn ids() -> int:
    yield 1
    yield 2
    names = [String("a")]      # allocates after the second resume
    yield names.len()

@noalloc
fn first_two() -> int:
    g = ids()
    a = g.next().unwrap()      # <- the body "up to the next yield": nothing allocates here
    b = g.next().unwrap()      # nor here, read literally; a third call would. The compiler cannot know which call a `next()` is in a loop, so it must choose: the segment (unsound for a loop) or the whole body (refuses `first_two`). The text picks neither.
    return a + b
findings.why: [EFF-1]: "Calling a generator runs none of its body; each `next` carries the effects of the body up to the next `yield`, and dropping a suspended one those of the drops it performs (ODR-057)." A `next` in a loop, or after a `next` another function made, reaches any segment; [EFF-5] checks a contract over the function's effect set, so the choice decides whether `first_two` is `E4001`.
findings.proposed_text: In `[EFF-1]`, replace "each `next` carries the effects of the body up to the next `yield`" with: "each `next` carries the effects of the whole body, the union over its segments, since which segment resumes is a state the program computes while it runs (a generator a `@noalloc` function drives therefore allocates nowhere in its body)".
findings.codes: E4001 and the other contract codes reused; the chain names the `yield` segment

findings.title: `[ARN-1]` says `scope()` ends every view into the arena; `[ARN-7]` ends views only where bytes are reused
findings.program:
fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(4096)
    cmds = ref mut frame.alloc_zeroed[int](8)
    with s = frame.scope():        # [ARN-1]: `scope()` "ends every view into the arena": `cmds` is ended here
        tmp = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[int](4)

findings.why: [ARN-1]: "`reset()`, `scope()` (`[ARN-6]`) and the arena's end may reuse or free that memory: each ends every view into the arena, and a later use of one is `E3060`." So the loop in `run_all` never reads freed memory for this program. The general hole stands, and it is O1's shape for summaries and contracts: `[EFF-2]` "it is every lambda and named function the program puts in that place, a library's included" and "For an interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method, it is every implementation and override the program has" are whole-program facts; `[EFF-4]` and `[BLD-14]` item 7 record only "the function values the package stores into a function type ... which a program that uses the package counts wherever such a value is called", the library-to-dependant direction; no sentence counts a dependant's store at the library's own call line (`h()` in `run_all`), which `[BLD-1]` compiles once, and `[EFF-25]` decides `E3020` there. Variants the text accepts and that break: a handler that changes another list `run_all` walks (`static mut OTHER` reached through `pub fn push_other`), and the contract half (`run_all` `@noalloc`, `Handler` without a contract: `[EFF-6]`'s "whole reachable call graph" is unseen by `bus`). One part of the reader's rule is wrong: a function-typed *parameter* is already compiled per function given by the package that gives it (`[COST-3]`: "a library function given a function is one instance per function, as Rust's generic `F: FnMut`"; `[EFF-4]`: "worked out for each instance, by the package that compiles that instance"), so parameters need no edge rule.

Parameters are not part of the hole.
verdicts.better_fix:
Add after `[EFF-2]`:

* `[EFF-2a]` **A place another package can fill.** A function-typed parameter is compiled once per function given, by the package that gives it, as a generic is (`[EFF-4]`, `[COST-3]`), so every function reaching it is seen where its line compiles. Every other place a function value is called through, and every `virtual` or interface method, is compiled by the package that declares it, which sees only its own stores and overrides (`[EFF-2]`). Where another package can fill such a place (a `pub` field, a `pub static`, an element of a list or map one of them holds, a place a `pub` function stores a function-typed parameter into, and every place a value from one of these is copied into), override such a method (a `virtual` method of a `pub` class) or implement it (a method of a `pub` interface called through `dyn`), a call through it counts, beside the functions this package puts there, a function another package may put there: one that may call every `pub` function of this package, change and end every place a `pub` name of this package reaches (a `pub static mut`; the fields of an object a `pub` function is given, returns or holds), take every lock a `pub` function takes, and have every effect the place's or method's declared contracts do not exclude (verdict 106). A place or method no other package can reach keeps `[EFF-2]`'s rule, and so does a `virtual` method of a class that cannot be subclassed outside its package. The message names the route: `E3020` "`h()` (line 11) may add to `HANDLERS` (through `add`, which a function another package stores into a `Handler` may call) while this loop walks `HANDLERS` (line 10); walk a list of your own: write `todo = mem.take(ref mut HANDLERS)` above line 10, `for h in todo:` in place of line 10, and `HANDLERS.extend(owns todo)` below the loop"; `E4001` "`run_all` is `@noalloc`, and `h()` (line 11) may run a function another package stores into a `Handler`; say what a `Handler` may do: write `@noalloc` above `type Handler = fn()`". A dependant's stores and overrides are counted by the dependant at its own lines (`[EFF-4]`, `[CLO-17]`), and `[DET-3]` counts the same way.

In `[BLD-14]` add item 8: "for each `pub` function, the places each of its function-typed parameters flows into (`[EFF-2]`: 'a place a value is copied into'), so that a dependant checks `[CLO-17]` at the call that hands the function over".
